title: Organelles and compartmentalization; Cell specialization

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Organelle
items.clue: A discrete subunit of a cell that is adapted to perform a specific function.

items.label: Differentiation
items.clue: The development of an unspecialized cell into a specialized cell with a particular structure and function.

items.label: Multipotent stem cell
items.clue: A stem cell that can differentiate into only a limited range of cell types, typically the cell types of one tissue.

items.label: Pluripotent stem cell
items.clue: A stem cell that can differentiate into any of the cell types of the body of the organism but not into the extra-embryonic tissues such as the placenta.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly applies the term organelle as it is used in IB Biology?

options.text: The plasma membrane is an organelle, although it forms the boundary of the cytoplasm.
Ribosomes are not organelles, because they are not bounded by a membrane.
The cell wall is an organelle, because it is a labelled part with a function.
The cytoskeleton is an organelle, because it is a structure that moves organelles.

questions.explanation: An organelle is a discrete subunit of a cell adapted to a specific function. The plasma membrane is such a unit, controlling exchange with the surroundings, and the guide lists it with nuclei, vesicles and ribosomes as an organelle.

questions.stem: A gene from a eukaryote is inserted into a bacterium and is transcribed there. In the eukaryotic cell the mRNA from this gene would be modified before translation. What happens to the mRNA in the bacterium?

options.text: It is modified in the cytoplasm before ribosomes can bind it.
It is translated inside the nucleoid before it is released.
It is not translated, as bacterial ribosomes read the DNA.
It is translated at once, without any modification.

questions.explanation: In prokaryotes there is no nuclear membrane separating transcription from translation, so mRNA may immediately meet ribosomes and be translated, even while it is still being transcribed. Post-transcriptional modification is not possible.

questions.stem: In a human, a neuron and a liver cell are both descended by mitosis from the same zygote. What is the difference between them once they have differentiated?

options.text: They express different subsets of the same complete set of genes.
They have kept different sets of genes and discarded the rest.
They were set on different paths inside from fertilization.
They differ only until the body needs to swap them over.

questions.stem: Which pair of properties defines a stem cell?

options.text: Ability to divide whenever a tissue is damaged and to produce more cells of its own type.
Ability to switch from one specialized type to another whenever a tissue requires this.
Capacity to divide endlessly and ability to differentiate along different pathways.
Continuous division at all times, giving new cells whether or not they are needed.

questions.explanation: These are the two defining properties in the guide: a stem cell can divide endlessly, and it can differentiate along different pathways to give specialized cell types. Both are required.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes pluripotent stem cells from totipotent stem cells?

options.text: Pluripotent cells can form any cell type of the body but not extra-embryonic tissues such as the placenta.
Pluripotent and totipotent cells can both form every cell type, so the two terms are interchangeable.
Pluripotent cells are the stem cells found in adult tissues such as bone marrow and hair follicles.
Pluripotent cells appear only after birth, since all the cells of an embryo remain totipotent.

questions.stem: Which statement about the range of cell size in humans is correct?

options.text: Red and white blood cells and gametes are all about 10 µm across.
The egg and the sperm are similar in size, as each supplies half the DNA.
A motor neuron can be over a metre long, yet only micrometres wide.
A muscle fibre several centimetres long must be a chain of short cells.

questions.explanation: Cell size is an aspect of specialization. A single motor neuron running from the spinal cord to a muscle in the foot has an axon over a metre long, while its width remains microscopic; extreme length suits its function of carrying signals over a distance.

questions.stem: A cube of side 1 mm has a surface area of 6 mm², a volume of 1 mm³ and a surface area-to-volume ratio of 6. The side length is increased to 4 mm. What is the new surface area-to-volume ratio?

options.text: 6, because the surface area and the volume are both multiplied by four
24, because a larger cube has more surface, so the ratio rises fourfold
0.67, because it compares the 64 mm³ volume with the 96 mm² surface area
1.5, because the area becomes 96 mm² and the volume becomes 64 mm³

questions.stem: A single-celled organism is growing. Why can it not keep growing indefinitely without dividing?

options.text: Its volume, which sets its need for exchange, grows faster than the surface through which exchange occurs.
Its surface area-to-volume ratio rises as it grows, until the membrane cannot hold the cell together.
Its larger surface area increases its need for materials until supply cannot keep up with demand.
Its surface area and volume increase by the same factor, so the limit must come from the nucleus instead.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly matches an adaptation of the chloroplast to its function in photosynthesis?

options.text: The thylakoid membranes provide a large surface area in which photosystems are held to absorb light.
The fluid inside the thylakoids contains the enzymes of the Calvin cycle at high concentration.
The stroma holds the photosystems in solution so that light can reach them from every direction.
The thylakoids enclose a large volume of water to act as the substrate for photolysis.

questions.stem: A cell is treated with a substance that blocks all of its nuclear pores. Which consequence would follow?

options.text: DNA could no longer leave the nucleus to be translated by the ribosomes in the cytoplasm.
Protein synthesis would carry on, as ribosomes inside the nucleus would translate the mRNA there.
mRNA could no longer leave the nucleus, so cytoplasmic ribosomes would receive no new mRNA.
mRNA and proteins would still cross the envelope, diffusing through its bilayers as small molecules do.

questions.stem: What is the role of clathrin in the formation of a vesicle?

options.text: It lines the inside of the vesicle so that it can bind and hold the cargo molecules that are being transported.
It is the membrane receptor protein that recognises and binds the substance that is to be brought into the cell.
It assembles into a lattice on the cytoplasmic side of the membrane, bending it into a pit that pinches off.
It builds a new membrane around the cargo, separate from the existing membrane, to enclose it.

questions.stem: Which features of a proximal convoluted tubule cell increase its surface area-to-volume ratio, and how?

options.text: Microvilli, which beat to sweep the filtrate across the cell so that more of it can be absorbed.
A small cell size, because shape cannot alter the ratio of a cell that has a given volume.
Its large size, because a bigger cell has more surface and so a higher surface area-to-volume ratio.
Microvilli and basal invaginations, which add membrane area without adding volume.

questions.stem: How are type I and type II pneumocytes adapted to their functions in the alveolar epithelium?

options.text: Type I cells are extremely thin for a short diffusion distance; type II cells hold many lamellar bodies that discharge surfactant.
Type II cells are the thicker gas-exchange cells; type I cells are thin cells that line the gaps between them.
Type I cells secrete surfactant from their lamellar bodies; type II cells are thin to allow rapid diffusion.
Type I and type II cells are one cell type at two stages, with the thin type I cells maturing into type II cells.

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly matches an adaptation of a human gamete to its function?

options.text: Sperm acrosome: stores the fuel that the mitochondria respire while the sperm swims.
Egg zona pellucida: a cell wall that gives the egg mechanical protection from damage.
Egg and sperm of matching size: each gamete carries half of the chromosomes needed.
Egg cytoplasm with nutrient stores: supplies the embryo's first divisions.

questions.explanation: The egg is large because its cytoplasm contains stored nutrients (yolk droplets) that supply the embryo during its first divisions, before it can obtain nutrients from the mother. This is why the egg is one of the largest human cells.
